label: Speed
title: Speed
headline: Can you stop within what you can see?
intro: Night falls fast on Namibia's open roads, and cattle, donkeys and kudu don't stay off them. See how your speed decides whether you can stop in time.

contentNotice.text: This experience talks about the risk of being killed or seriously injured in a crash. It uses diagrams and charts, not crash images.

scenes.question: Cattle, donkeys and dogs often wander onto Namibian roads. How many collisions with domestic animals were recorded from {n:2020} to {n:2025}?

art.alt: A tarred two-lane road through dry bushveld at dusk, with farm fences on both sides.

lines: Friday evening. You're driving home to Otjiwarongo on a quiet tarred road.
The sun has gone down. You switch your headlights on.
Farm fences line the road, but there are gaps. Cattle sometimes get through.

scenes.prompt: The limit on this road is {claim:na.law.speed-tar}. What speed will you drive at?
Dipped headlights only have to light up {claim:na.law.dippedbeam} of road. A cow is standing in your lane, just where the light ends. Can you stop in time?

art.alt: Night on the same road. Dipped headlights light a short stretch ahead. A cow is standing in your lane at the edge of the light.

scenes.title: How far you travel before you stop (dry tar)
scenes.caption: Dipped beams must light at least {claim:na.law.dippedbeam}, main beams at least {claim:na.law.mainbeam}. At night on dipped beams, only the slowest of these speeds stops within the light.

scenes.title: Risk of a fatal crash compared with driving at {n:80} km/h
scenes.caption: Small increases add up fast. The WHO says each {n:1%} rise in average speed brings about a {claim:int.who.speed-1pct} rise in the risk of a fatal crash.

scenes.explain: {claim:na.stat.animal-collisions} collisions with domestic animals were recorded from {n:2020} to {n:2025}, mostly with cattle, donkeys and dogs. Wild animals like kudu add to the risk at dusk and at night.

scenes.title: If an animal is on the road

steps.title: Slow down early
steps.body: When you see animals near the road, or warning signs, slow down before you reach them. Where there's one, there are often more.

steps.title: Brake firmly, in a straight line
steps.body: Keep the car straight while you brake. A sudden swerve at speed can roll a vehicle or send it into oncoming traffic.

steps.title: Look for eyeshine
steps.body: At night, animals' eyes reflect your lights before you can make out their shape. Treat any pair of bright dots as an animal.

steps.title: Use main beam, and dip it in time
steps.body: On empty roads, main beam shows you more. The law says you must dip it if it could dazzle an oncoming driver. Switch back once they've passed.

lines: Drive at a speed that lets you stop within the distance you can see.
At night on dipped beams, that distance is short. Slow down.
If an animal is in the road, brake hard in a straight line. Don't swerve.

scenes.title: The last stretch home
scenes.label: A made-up story, based on common situations
scenes.warning: This story mentions a crash and an injury. It doesn't describe the injury in detail.
paragraphs: Tomas had driven the road to his uncle's farm a hundred times. He knew every bend, so he drove it fast, even after dark.
One night a donkey was standing in the road, just beyond his lights. He braked, but there wasn't enough road left. The bakkie hit the donkey and left the road.
Tomas spent weeks in hospital and months learning to walk without pain. 'I knew the road,' he says now. 'I didn't know what was on it that night.'
These days he drives the farm road slower after dark, and he waits for the morning when he can.

signpost.text: If a crash has affected you or someone close to you, you don't have to deal with it alone. LifeLine/ChildLine Namibia offers free counselling: call {claim:na.support.lifeline}.
